node_definition.done_when: Read design/canvas-layout-spec.md for type scale and spacing, but note the canvas topbar was drawn against a three-project fixture and cannot hold twelve, so this departs from it deliberately on the lead's instruction. FIVE PARTS, one node because the whole point is that one preference propagates — splitting this across files is what produced the r-3col defect earlier today, where a container's rules were retired in one scope and the container survived in another. ONE: the topbar becomes a single row — brand, project control, tabs, search, settings, snapshot receipt — with the tabs left-aligned after the project control. TWO: the Overview tab is removed. The brand button already calls navProject(null) titled All projects and renders the fleet page, and CockpitBody renders the same cross-project content, so they are two doors to one room; fold anything CockpitBody shows that the fleet view does not into the fleet view rather than dropping it, and leave the tabs as the four within-project views Plans, Sprints, Graph and Crew. THREE: the project control shows the current project with its live dot and opens a dropdown listing only VISIBLE projects, each with its plan count and live count, plus a Configure entry at the foot. FOUR: Configure opens the visibility panel that lives in the settings menu in docs/ui/_shared.jsx beside theme and density, which already own exactly this class of cross-cutting display preference — the dropdown entry is a shortcut that opens that same panel and must not be a second implementation of it. The panel lists every mounted project with a visible or hidden toggle. FIVE: visibility propagates. It is read today only by shell.jsx for the chip strip; crew.jsx and the fleet strip never see it. Every fleet-wide display must respect it: the Crew run list, the Overview fleet statistics, and any other cross-project aggregate. Distinguish mounted from shown where a count is displayed, since twelve mounted and three shown are different facts. CRITICAL AND SUBTLE: hidden means excluded from aggregates and from the selector shortcut list; it must never mean unreachable. Any mounted project stays reachable through Configure and through the command palette — a project being hidden is why nova could not be selected, and that bug is a display preference wrongly used as a routing filter. A test asserts the topbar renders one row containing the tabs with no Overview tab, that the dropdown lists visible projects only and offers Configure, that Configure and the settings menu render the same panel rather than two, that hiding a project removes it from the Crew list and the fleet statistics while leaving it selectable through the palette, and that a count displaying mounted and shown reports both. The existing suite passes unchanged.
node_definition.goal: Make project visibility one fleet-wide setting that every surface respects, and fit the topbar on one row

node_definition.done_when: Two sessions independently watched finished runs display as working: one saw six nodes whose worker processes had all exited and whose manifests were all terminal on disk sit as '6 working' for 38 minutes with zero events, and one saw a run whose classifier read completed_unpromoted with a complete manifest while its phase still read starting. The mechanism is in reckon/crew/recovery.py and has two parts that compound. First, in classify_pointer around lines 186 to 196, when the process appears alive AND the log file's mtime is newer than the manifest's, the manifest is discarded wholesale: manifest_present set false, manifest_data emptied, manifest_status set to empty string. That staleness heuristic is right for a manifest written mid-run and then superseded, but it is wrong for a TERMINAL status: complete, blocked and failed are facts a later log line cannot undo, and discarding them is what erases the strongest completion signal available. Second, in _watch_snapshot around lines 556 to 578, state resolves to dispatched when phase is starting and the stall check that follows is gated on state being exactly working, while FLEET_WORKING_STATES at line 610 counts dispatched among the working bucket. So a run that dies before its phase advances is counted as alive and is permanently ineligible for the stall check. Fix both, leading with the manifest because it turns a timing question into a fact-on-disk question: never discard a terminal manifest status through the staleness path, and evaluate the stall check over every non-terminal state rather than working alone. Tests in tests/test_crew_finished_display.py assert: a pointer whose manifest reports complete while its log is newer and its process appears alive still resolves to a terminal state rather than dispatched, and the same for blocked and failed; a run killed immediately after dispatch, before its phase ever advances past starting, is still detected from its manifest alone; a run with no manifest and no activity past the stall window resolves to stalled from the dispatched state, which it cannot today; and a genuinely mid-run pointer whose manifest is non-terminal and whose log is newer still has that manifest treated as superseded, so the staleness heuristic is narrowed rather than removed. Your gate is that new test file plus tests/test_crew_recovery.py, tests/test_crew_ticker.py and tests/test_crew_watch_stream.py. Do NOT run the full suite and do NOT run any browser-driven test. That is the resumed-worker case and it is well exercised: this ledger holds 49 runs with attempt_kind resume, and three runs in this session alone went blocked then working after a resume. The distinction the previous change missed is that complete and failed are VERDICTS a later log line cannot undo, while blocked is a SOLICITATION that resume answers, and the discard is how the system notices it was answered. Narrow the exclusion set to complete and failed only, so a blocked manifest is discardable again under the unchanged surrounding conditions of an alive process and a newer log, while complete and failed remain protected as 1b7e72e intended. Add to tests/test_crew_finished_display.py: a blocked manifest with an alive process and a newer log resolves to working rather than blocked, named for the resumed worker it represents; a blocked manifest with a DEAD process or an older log still resolves blocked, so the fix does not simply delete the signal; and the existing complete and failed protections still hold, which the parametrised test already covers and must keep passing. Your gate is tests/test_crew_finished_display.py plus tests/test_crew_recovery.py, tests/test_crew_ticker.py and tests/test_crew_watch_stream.py, which were 28 passed at 8692c0aa245b82ed05ce46c108f6729abf261203. node_definition.done_when: reckon/crew/promotion.py appends the ledger row and deletes the live pointer, in that order so an interruption stays recoverable, and releases nothing else: the run's worktree survives until someone runs crew gc by hand and the worker process survives until it exits on its own. Measured on this workstation: 274 worktrees on disk against 458 promoted runs in one ledger, and a run observed process_alive true while its classification already read completed_unpromoted. Extend complete so that AFTER the ledger append and the pointer delete it also releases the run's own worktree and, if still alive, the run's own process group. Reuse the classification crew gc already applies in reckon/crew/routing.py rather than writing a second policy: a worktree is released only when git status --porcelain in it reports zero entries AND its HEAD is an ancestor of the integration branch as git merge-base --is-ancestor decides; a worktree failing either condition is left in place and never removed with force; and a shadow releases through the existing lineage rule against its committed record and retained patch. The process group is signalled only when a terminal manifest was delivered, because a live process with no manifest is a recovery case rather than a cleanup one. Every withheld release is named in the returned completion result with the condition it failed, so a retained worktree is visible at the moment it is created rather than discovered by a later path collision. A failure inside the release step must never undo or obscure the ledger append. Tests in tests/test_promotion_release.py assert: a promoted run whose worktree reports zero porcelain entries and whose HEAD is an ancestor of the integration branch leaves no worktree on disk and no live process, asserted through complete end to end rather than by unit-testing a helper; a promoted run whose worktree reports a porcelain entry keeps that worktree and names it in the result with the failed condition; one whose HEAD is not an ancestor of the integration branch does the same; a run with no terminal manifest is never signalled; and a simulated failure raised inside the release step still leaves the promoted ledger row intact and the run recoverable. The mechanism is in reckon/crew/recovery.py and has two parts that compound. First, in classify_pointer around lines 186 to 196, when the process appears alive AND the log file's mtime is newer than the manifest's, the manifest is discarded wholesale: manifest_present set false, manifest_data emptied, manifest_status set to empty string. That staleness heuristic is right for a manifest written mid-run and then superseded, but it is wrong for a TERMINAL status: complete, blocked and failed are facts a later log line cannot undo, and discarding them is what erases the strongest completion signal available. Second, in _watch_snapshot around lines 556 to 578, state resolves to dispatched when phase is starting and the stall check that follows is gated on state being exactly working, while FLEET_WORKING_STATES at line 610 counts dispatched among the working bucket. So a run that dies before its phase advances is counted as alive and is permanently ineligible for the stall check. Fix both, leading with the manifest because it turns a timing question into a fact-on-disk question: never discard a terminal manifest status through the staleness path, and evaluate the stall check over every non-terminal state rather than working alone. node_definition.done_when: The recovery order has been recorded in this workstation's guidance since the first incident and was not applied at the second, four hours later, by a different session - so guidance that must be recalled at the moment of an incident has already failed twice. It is now written where a coordinator is already reading. TWO FILES, AND THE LEAD DIRECTED BOTH. reckon/crew/AGENTS.md is the narrowest scope owning crew dispatch and the command surface, and gains a recovery section. A new reference under the ship skill's references directory carries the operational detail, linked from the skill's own text in the same beat so it is reachable rather than orphaned - read that SKILL.md before writing, and follow how its existing references are introduced. WHAT BOTH MUST STATE, and each claim below is measured rather than asserted, so reproduce the figures. THE CAUSE: a per-request provider refusal kills the turn without killing the session; the run classifies blocked, its worktree survives, and its session remains on disk. THE TRAP: session_id null on a live pointer means only that observe has not run, never that a run is unresumable - resume_plan recovers it from the stream by itself. Two coordinators read that null as a verdict on the same day; the first promoted five runs, the second left one blocked for five hours and forty-two minutes. THE ORDER: inspect the worktree for committed and uncommitted work, resume the session, and reconcile only once resume is impossible - because promotion deletes the pointer and takes the resume path with it. THE COUNTER-INSTINCTS, both of which are wrong and both of which were followed: promoting first to tidy the fleet destroys what you were about to recover; and re-observing a refused run to investigate a hold used to renew it, which is fixed but explains the habit. WHAT IS SAFE DURING A HOLD: observe reads the local stream and never calls the provider, so it works mid-refusal - confirmed on two sessions' runs tonight, and the opposite belief would teach a reader to panic when panic is unwarranted. THE AUTOMATIC PATH: a sweep resumes lapsed holds on a cadence from the follow loop, and a follower started before that code landed will never run it, so a follower is cycled when recovery code lands. THE COMMANDS as they exist when this lands, verified by running each with --help rather than copied from this brief, since two of them are being added by concurrent nodes and one existing crew recover does something else entirely. Do not restate the plan; link it. node_definition.done_when: THE TIMER IS SELF-EXTENDING AND A RETRY LOOP CANNOT CONVERGE. Measured tonight from this repository's committed ledger, data.holds: a claude dispatch hold opened 20:02:18Z and closed 23:52:19Z, held_seconds 13801, three hours fifty minutes on a lane that was serving. The control sits beside it - a claude-opus resume hold, held_seconds 83, closed the moment one served run reached that backend. The two differ only in whether traffic reached that specific backend. Every refused resume re-stamps the backend's budget record, so a caller retrying on any cadence shorter than the shelf life pushes the expiry ahead of itself, and observing the refused run does the same because its stream carries the rejection - the obvious check-before-believing move makes it worse. AVAILABILITY IS POLLED RATHER THAN READ FROM WRITTEN EVIDENCE, which is this workstation's standing direction, and this is the case that forces it: a timer answers only whether enough time has passed that a lane might serve, while one cheap request answers whether it does. Done when a hold whose refusal names no reset time is unknown-until-probed rather than exhausted-until-a-clock: the fence probes that backend with a minimal request and the probe's result, not the record's age, decides whether the wave opens. A served probe clears the hold and records the served observation so the next caller reads a fact rather than repeating the probe; a refused probe re-arms the hold and records that refusal as the new evidence. THE PROBE MUST NOT BECOME THE COST IT PREVENTS: rate-limited per backend so a wave of held dispatches issues one probe rather than one each, its result cached for a bounded interval that is itself configuration, and a backend that has never reported anything is still never held, because absence of a signal remains not evidence of exhaustion. node_definition.done_when: A crew follow process holds the module code it imported for its entire life. When a recovery sweep landed and was wired into that loop, every follower on this workstation had started hours earlier, so not one called it - two independent sessions were simultaneously unable to perform a recovery they had just gained, and one left a run blocked five hours forty-two minutes with its limit long lifted. The failure is silent in the costly direction: a stale renderer draws a wrong column and someone notices, while a stale follower recovers nothing and is indistinguishable from a fleet with nothing to recover. THREE SHAPES IN THE ORDER TO TRY THEM, and the plan states this order deliberately. First, the follower detects that the installed package on disk is newer than the one it imported and re-execs itself in place, preserving its session registration and its stdout so a watching pane sees no gap. Second, if in-place re-exec cannot preserve those, the watch seat publishes a version stamp each cycle and a follower reading a stamp newer than its own re-execs. Third, only if neither is achievable, the follower emits one line saying it is stale and how to cycle it - this is a fallback, not the answer, because the done-when requires an operator who never restarts a follower to still get new behaviour. Report which shape you implemented and why the earlier ones were not achievable if you fell back. THE DETECTION MUST NOT BE THE PACKAGE VERSION STRING: reckon's __version__ is dynamic via vcs and frozen at install, so it does not move when a working-tree edit lands - a watch-seat stamp built on it was already landed and measured inert across eighty-five commits. So the price is either a NEW NODE ID, which makes one piece of work appear as two unrelated ledger rows, or a MANUAL WORKTREE REMOVAL. BOTH PRICES ARE PAID IN THE CURRENCY THIS SYSTEM SPENT THE NIGHT PROTECTING: manual worktree removal is the act that turned a ten-minute provider outage into a loss of five recoverable sessions, and crew complete now refuses to promote a blocked run whose session is recoverable precisely to prevent it - so the switching path routes a careful operator toward the one action the rest of the system guards against. And crew resume accepts no backend override, so a run whose lane is genuinely spent cannot be continued elsewhere at all. That case is live: a run on another project is held by a usage limit resetting four days out, so resume never becomes available for it and a lane change is the only lawful move. THE SHAPE IS LOCKED as the plan's lane-change-verb decision: BOTH entry points over ONE implementation - a backend override on resume for a blocked run whose lane is spent, and a redispatch keeping the node id for a working run the coordinator wants elsewhere - because each covers a state the other cannot and two implementations would be two code paths able to disagree about one run. Done when a dispatched run moves to another backend keeping its node id, its worktree and its ledger identity, with no manual tree removal and no new node id; when the move records BOTH lanes and the reason on the run, so its history shows where it ran rather than appearing to have always run on the second; when a move onto a held lane is refused with the hold named, since the sweep's own rule is never to spend the last of a recovering quota; and when a session that cannot follow the move because the new backend is a different harness is reported as starting fresh rather than silently losing its context - that report is the load-bearing negative, because a silent context loss here is the same defect as a promotion reporting success while discarding a session. ASSERT THROUGH THE COMMANDS a coordinator invokes, over a dispatched run built the way dispatch writes one under a temporary config home with the real config home asserted untouched: the node id and worktree path unchanged afterwards, the ledger carrying both lanes, a move onto a held lane refused naming the hold, and a cross-harness move reporting the fresh start. Assert both entry points reach the same implementation. At least one added assertion must fail against base ff0a594. Measured over tests/test_crew_lane_change.py plus tests/test_crew_dispatch_guard.py in ONE invocation: zero failures against their combined count at base. Report ruff findings on the staged paths against the count at base.

Bisected: it passes at b06b68b^ and fails at b06b68b, the manifest-is-not-a-verdict change - so a run whose manifest reads complete and whose process has exited now classifies as ABANDONED rather than completed-unpromoted. THAT IS THE MOST EXPENSIVE MISCLASSIFICATION THIS SURFACE CAN PRODUCE and it is the inverse of the defect b06b68b was written to fix. Abandoned invites a coordinator to discard; completed-unpromoted invites them to promote; and such a run has finished work in its worktree that nobody has landed - so the label routes a reader toward destroying delivered work, which three separate guards were built this week to prevent. The live fleet is currently unaffected, measured at completed_unpromoted 1 and abandoned 0 across eleven real pointers, so the fixture reaches a manifest-and-liveness combination production does not - a latent regression rather than an active one, and not a reason to relax the fix. THE FIX MUST NOT UNDO b06b68b: a placeholder failed or blocked manifest must still render as running while the pid is alive, which is what that change bought and what a peer confirmed from two independent cases. Done when a run whose manifest status is complete and whose process has exited classifies as completed-unpromoted; when a placeholder failed manifest over a LIVE process still classifies as running, asserted so the earlier fix cannot be reverted by this one; when a run with no manifest and a dead process still classifies as abandoned, so that label stays reachable; and when the three-class fixture counts one of each. State in the code why complete over a dead process is a verdict while failed over a live process is not, because the asymmetry is the point and a later reader will otherwise flatten it. Record in reckon/crew/AGENTS.md that a node touching reckon/crew/recovery.py or reckon/mcp.py carries tests/test_ledger.py in its gate, since that module holds cross-cutting contracts - this classification count and the five-tool surface assertion - and has now caught two changes fenced away from it. node_definition.done_when: pytest tests/test_local_lane_refusal_signal.py -q passes, and a stream that died of rate limiting no longer reports that it carries no rate-limit event. THE DEFECT, measured tonight across four dead runs in two projects: reckon/_backends.py line 852 reads exactly one record kind for budget, "elif kind == rate_limit_event", and nothing in that module reads api_retry or error_status. The clive local backend never emits rate_limit_event. It emits api_retry records carrying error_status 429 and error rate_limit. So a run that died of rate limiting is recorded with budget detail "no rate-limit event in the stream yet", refusal false, headroom unknown. The documented rule is that unknown headroom never holds a wave, and correctly so, which means the fence cannot fire at any level of local exhaustion and the next wave dispatches into the lane that just shed workers. This is a guard that cannot fire, which outranks a guard that fires wrongly: a stale hold announces itself while a blind one is indistinguishable from a clear lane. THE SHAPES, measured rather than assumed. Exhaustion: many api_retry records then a terminal result record carrying subtype success together with is_error true. Mid-flight death: api_retry records and no terminal result record at all. DO NOT key on a retry count of ten. Ten is the retry budget for a single API call, not for a run; two dead runs here carry 15 and 18 api_retry records and two in another project carry 10 and 5, so any constant matches some exhaustions and misses others, which is the worst behaviour available to a fence. Read the count as a magnitude and the terminal shape as the verdict. THE FALSIFIER, and it is the assertion that matters most: retrying is not refusing. Two runs that completed normally tonight each carried SEVEN api_retry records and finished with real work committed. A change that treats any api_retry as a refusal would mark every busy lane spent and hold the whole fleet, and it would pass any test that only checks the dead runs. Assert both directions: a stream with retries that ends in a genuine success reports no refusal and does not hold; a stream whose retries end in the exhaustion shape reports a refusal with a stated reason naming rate limiting; a stream with no retries at all is unchanged; and the existing rate_limit_event path for other backends keeps working exactly as it does now. Measure base and head over tests/test_local_lane_refusal_signal.py plus every test importing reckon._backends; report failure ids either side and require none added.
node_definition.goal: Teach the budget observer to see the exhaustion signal the local lane actually writes, so a spent local lane can be known before the next wave enters it

node_definition.done_when: pytest tests/test_closure_fence_agreement.py -q passes, and no pointer is reconciled on one surface and unreconciled on the other. THE DEFECT, measured by an imas-codex fleet and confirmed here at the source: two independent definitions of one word, neither consulting the other. reckon/crew/runs.py drain, around line 823, treats a pointer as reconciled when its recorded closure_disposition is handed-off, or still-working while its classification is running; for handed-off it consults neither age nor classification, and its docstring states that intent plainly, that a handoff remains valid until the receiving session reconciles the pointer. reckon/crew/recovery.py overdue_unreconciled_runs, around line 873, treats a pointer as unreconciled when its classification is completed_unpromoted or blocked and its terminal age exceeds the configured grace, and it never reads closure_disposition at all. So a terminal pointer past grace carrying a valid handed-off disposition is reconciled by drain and refused by dispatch with exit 6. That fleet measured exactly this on three pointers at once. WHY IT IS NOT A DISPLAY NIT: the ship skill instructs a coordinator to read the drain view and require unreconciled-runs zero before ending a session, so the fence a closure signature rests on is the permissive one. Their outgoing coordinator signed a sprint closure on that zero and committed it, attesting to a state the other surface denies. A fence satisfiable on one surface and refused on the other is not a fence. THE FIX: have overdue_unreconciled_runs consult the same recorded disposition drain does, through one shared predicate both call, so the two agree by construction rather than by two authors agreeing. Do not simply widen dispatch to ignore the pointers. THE PROTECTION THAT MUST SURVIVE, and these are the load-bearing assertions: a terminal pointer past grace carrying NO disposition is still refused by dispatch, because that is the forgotten-work case the fence exists for; a still-working disposition on a pointer that has since gone terminal excuses nothing on either surface, since drain already expires that and dispatch must not become the weaker of the two; and a handed-off pointer is reconciled on BOTH surfaces. Assert additionally that for a set of pointers mixing all three cases, the count drain reports and the count dispatch refuses on are equal. A change that merely relaxes dispatch would pass the third assertion and destroy the first. Measure base and head over tests/test_closure_fence_agreement.py plus every test importing reckon.crew.recovery or reckon.crew.runs; report failure ids either side and require none added.
node_definition.goal: Make the closure fence and the dispatch fence read one definition of unreconciled, so a session cannot be closed on a state dispatch denies

node_definition.done_when: pytest tests/test_lane_concurrency_ceiling.py -q passes, and a dispatch to a backend already carrying its ceiling of live runs is refused with a named, actionable reason instead of launching. WHY THIS IS THE PREVENTION AND NOT A NICETY, measured tonight: a peer dispatched a sixth concurrent worker to the local lane at 05:10 and within a minute TWO ALREADY-RUNNING runs died — each after ten 429 retries at up to 40 second spacing, one of them mid-gate with two commits in its worktree. Adding work destroyed work. The mechanism is not ours to fix downstream: the harness retry budget is fixed at max_retries 10 with 5 to 39 second backoff, reckon passes no retry configuration and cannot extend it, so once a lane refuses long enough the turn errors and a print-mode process exits. A 429 is a pause at the protocol; the finite retry budget is what converts it into a death. Therefore the only reliable remedy is not to create the overload. ADD A PER-BACKEND max_concurrent_runs to the flight backend entry, declared beside the existing per-backend keys (alias, command, effort, launch, model, sandbox, session_reuse, time_budget, usable_input_window) and validated in the schema. Absent or null means unlimited, which must remain the default for every backend that does not declare one, so this changes nothing for a lane nobody has measured. Count the backend live runs from the live pointers, count only non-terminal ones, and refuse when a new dispatch would exceed the ceiling. THE REFUSAL MUST BE ACTIONABLE, not a bare error: name the backend, the ceiling, the current count, and the run ids occupying the slots, so a coordinator can see what to wait for. Use the existing not-dispatchable exit convention rather than inventing a new one, and do not create a worktree or a process before refusing. FALSIFIERS, all required: a backend with no ceiling declared dispatches exactly as today, unlimited; a backend under its ceiling dispatches normally; a backend at its ceiling whose occupying runs are TERMINAL does not refuse, because a finished run holds no slot; and the refusal never touches a run already in flight. THAT LAST ONE IS THE POINT OF THE NODE: a fence that stopped an existing run in order to admit a new one would reproduce the harm it exists to prevent. Do not add a wait or retry loop inside dispatch; refusing is the whole behaviour, and the caller decides.
